title: On the Phenomenon of Bullshit Jobs
thesis: Modern economies can create roles that are socially prestigious, privately miserable, and hard to defend in honest language.
why: Provocative without being gimmicky: a clean argument about work, class, institutions, and self-deception that can unlock useful disagreement.

title: Seeing Like a State
thesis: Administrative systems simplify messy human realities into legible maps, and the simplification can become dangerous when paired with authority.
why: A durable lens for politics, cities, schools, investing data, family systems, and agentic OS design alike.

title: Men Explain Things to Me
thesis: Authority often reproduces itself through who feels entitled to explain, interrupt, certify, or dismiss another person's reality.
why: A compact social essay with enough bite to be worth rereading even when you disagree with parts of its downstream cultural life.

title: The Mosquito Strategy
thesis: Disease control can look less like heroic medicine and more like patient engineering, incentives, and delivery infrastructure.
why: A high-signal progress-studies read that is practical, humane, and far from the usual AI discourse.

title: The Problem With Everything-Bagel Liberalism
source: Ezra Klein / The New York Times
thesis: When every policy tries to carry every value at once, good projects can become too slow, too expensive, and too fragile to happen.
why: Useful as a live operating principle for Austin, housing, infrastructure, and personal project design.

title: A Simple Plan to Solve All of America's Problems
thesis: A politics that can build enough homes, energy, medicine, and infrastructure may matter more than a politics that only redistributes scarcity.
why: A strong bridge between family economics, Austin growth, climate/energy, and institutional competence.

title: The Weirdest People in the World?
source: Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine, Ara Norenzayan / Behavioral and Brain Sciences
frame: Psychology, culture, and hidden sample bias
thesis: Much of what psychology treats as universal may be unusually shaped by Western, educated, industrialized, rich, democratic populations.
why: A worldview-shifting research essay for thinking about parenting, religion, markets, institutions, and what evidence really proves.

title: The Market for Lemons
source: George Akerlof / Quarterly Journal of Economics
thesis: When sellers know quality and buyers cannot verify it, bad goods can drive out good ones even when everyone is acting rationally.
why: A classic that keeps paying rent across investing, hiring, marketplaces, healthcare, education, and AI-agent evaluation.

title: June 2026 Investing Newsletter: The Wild West
thesis: A secondary macro-investing read that ties liquidity, fiscal constraints, market structure, and asset allocation into one investable frame.
why: Keep one market-thesis lane in the mix, but as a counterweight rather than the whole menu.

title: Finance as a Scale-Invariant Global Computer
thesis: Markets can be read as a distributed computation layer, where every time horizon trades off speed, information, uncertainty, and capital allocation.
why: A finance essay with enough abstraction to connect to software, institutions, and decision systems.

title: Attack On Europe: Documenting Russian Equipment Losses
thesis: Open-source evidence can turn war from narrative fog into a grim but analyzable logistics and attrition ledger.
why: A different kind of long read: less essay, more epistemic method, useful for judging defense, geopolitics, and source reliability.

title: The Website Obesity Crisis
thesis: The web's everyday slowness is not inevitable; it reflects incentives, neglect, and a loss of craft discipline.
why: A funny, sharp software essay that doubles as a reminder to keep Alphalpha's own surfaces fast, clear, and humane.
